Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Visual (Fire/Flames): Fire or flames, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled

Vignette:
Mateo Rivera remembered the afternoon the sky turned the color of burnt copper, long before he ever would have associated that particular shade of orange with anything but an autumn evening. He was driving back from his brother’s house in the valley when the dry heat finally broke under a sudden windshift, carrying the sharp, acrid scent of burning pine and dry earth. The flames moved faster than the road signs warned, leaping from ridge to ridge with a crackling hunger that turned the daylight into a low, pulsing glow. He had pulled over, rolled down his windows, and watched the wind push the fire line closer, the heat pressing against his skin until he finally reversed, tires slipping on loose gravel, praying the ridge wouldn’t collapse. What frightened him most was the certainty that the weather itself had turned against him, that the same dry barometric drop and sudden gusts would decide whether he made it home. Over the months that followed, Mateo found himself circling the same moments in his head. He kept replaying the morning he left for work, dwelling on what he had done wrong, certain that leaving his grandfather’s woodpile unstacked or waiting for the fire department’s later call had cost him something irreplaceable. He ran through calculations of what could have prevented the loss: moving the livestock an hour earlier, sandbagging the lower drainage, hiring a crew to clear the perimeter. When the images grew too heavy, he learned to push them out of his mind, forcing his attention to the radio, to the road, to the simple mechanics of his own breathing, though the effort never fully cleared the air. Alongside these thoughts came a body that no longer trusted its own stillness. His chest would tighten, his pulse would hammer against his ribs, and his shoulders would rise until he was scanning every horizon for smoke, every cloud for the same shifting winds. He found himself jumping at the sudden whir of an oven fan or the sharp chime of a phone notification, his nerves already wound tight from watching the sky. At seventy-five, Mateo still worked as a QA Engineer, auditing regional environmental monitoring systems from his home office, where dual monitors displayed live sensor feeds and calibration logs. On a Tuesday morning in late July, the wind speed and humidity values on his weather dashboard shifted into a pattern identical to that disaster day. The dry heat reading climbed, the gust metric spiked, and Mateo felt his breath catch before he could stop it. His heart rate climbed, his palms grew damp, and he found himself scanning the secondary monitors for air quality anomalies, then glancing toward the street through his blinds as if checking for embers. When his desk phone rang, he flinched so sharply his chair scraped the floor. He began switching to archived datasets instead of reviewing live feeds, telling himself it was for data continuity, though the delay in his reports and the longer review times became noticeable to his supervisors. At home, he adjusted his routine, keeping the windows closed during certain hours, checking the local fire danger index twice before dinner, and sitting away from the space heater so he wouldn’t have to track its ignition cycle. Elena noticed the distance in his posture during meals, the way he would suddenly stop mid-sentence when a neighbor’s charcoal grill caught a draft, but they spoke of it only in practical terms. What finally brought him to seek help was the growing weight of his own physical toll and the fear that his days would keep shrinking under the weight of vigilance. He wanted to stop bracing for a sky that was already clear, hoping instead to sit at his desk without waiting for the wind to change, to sleep without listening for sirens, and to let himself believe that some days would simply be quiet.
